interview.hardest_part: Establishing any meaningful automated production before Death World biters overwhelm the character. The automation science pack chain (miner → furnaces → inserters → assemblers → labs) requires dozens of intermediate items and many navigation steps, all while biter waves escalate continuously. Each action is one second of wall-clock time including thinking, so the effective action budget across three hours is probably 1,500–2,500 steps after reasoning overhead — not enough to build a full automation loop on Marathon difficulty.
interview.likely_failure: Biter attack kills the character before a burner-miner setup is in place. On Death World the first wave arrives within a few in-game minutes, and without turrets or weapon upgrades the character has very limited staying power. The single-attempt rule means one unlucky encounter ends the run entirely. A secondary failure mode is spending the full time budget on manual mining and smelting without ever reaching automated_iron milestones, leaving the top half of the scorecard empty.
interview.helpful_mechanics: Hand mining with J counts toward produced.iron-ore immediately — no crafting or placement required, so the first ten or so iron-ore milestones are reachable in the first few hundred steps just by walking to a patch and holding J. Stone furnaces cost only 5 stone and smelt without electricity, so iron-plate and copper-plate milestones are accessible with minimal setup. Gear wheels are hand-craftable from plates with no machine required. The character spawns near starting ore patches on a fixed seed, so I can plan an efficient path rather than explore blind.
interview.harmful_mechanics: Death World substantially increases biter abundance, aggression, and expansion speed — the threat timeline is much shorter than a standard map, forcing defensive detours that consume a large fraction of the action budget. Marathon mode quadruples crafting costs and research costs, so every component of the automation chain takes far longer to assemble. The one-action-per-step constraint turns navigation into a major bottleneck: crossing even a modest distance to a distant ore patch or coal deposit eats dozens of steps. The 3-hour wall-clock limit includes thinking time, so the real action count is much lower than it appears. Finally, one attempt with no retry means any death resets all progress.
